rationale: This qualitative study (semi-structured interviews with 19 households, 3 community water informants, and 3 national/district officials, plus 2 focus group discussions across three rural Ghanaian communities) examines how decentralized community-based rural water governance operates across five capacity dimensions. Institutional structure and coordination is the overarching primary mechanism (decentralization of mandates and fiscal/training responsibilities from the national Community Water and Sanitation Agency to district assemblies and communities, alongside poor inter-agency coordination and unclear mandate delineation), co-equally analyzed alongside mandated community participation via voluntary Water and Sanitation Committees (including gender quotas) and O&M cost-recovery user fee rules (with secondary discussion of local bylaw and fee payment enforcement gaps), warranting 'multiple' for assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple. On the outcome side, the study primarily evaluates institutional/governance capacity and regulatory compliance outcomes across the five dimensions (e.g., non-compliance with water quality testing and gender composition rules, committee attrition, and uncoordinated data/mandates), while co-centrally documenting severe effective-access failures (frequent hand-pump borehole breakdowns leaving households without potable water for months and reliant on unmonitored streams), warranting 'administrative_outcome' as primary_outcome_family and 'multiple' for assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple.
